summary: Recommends against using the AS_SET and AS_CONFED_SET path segment types in BGP. Dropping them simplifies the design and implementation of BGP and makes the route origin clearer, which also helps work on secure routing. It is a best current practice, later replaced by RFC 9774.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6472 recommends that network operators stop announcing BGP routes with AS_SET or AS_CONFED_SET path segments. It says these segments obscure route-origin information and can hinder security and traffic-engineering work.

questions: should i use as_set in bgp
should operators announce as_set in bgp
subtitle: A best-practice recommendation against AS_SET and AS_CONFED_SET path segments.

tldr.problem: AS_SET and AS_CONFED_SET make route origin less clear and can complicate origin authentication and traffic engineering.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends that operators stop announcing routes containing these path segments and withdraw existing ones in favor of component-prefix routes without them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6472 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 9774.

today: RFC 6472 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 9774.

sections.title: Why These Path Segments Are a Problem
sections.content:
BGP's AS_PATH attribute records autonomous systems a route has traversed. When a router aggregates routes, AS_SET carries an unordered set of autonomous systems; AS_CONFED_SET carries an unordered set of member AS numbers within a confederation.

The RFC says this aggregation blurs which system originated a route. It can make origin authentication difficult, affect reachability for an aggregate and its component prefixes, and remove path detail useful for traffic engineering.
sections.plainLanguage: These path segments combine several routes but do not preserve their order. That makes the route's origin and the paths of its component prefixes less clear.

sections.title: The Limited Benefit of Aggregation
sections.content:
The RFC reports that AS_SET aggregation was very seldom used on the public network and, when used, was usually incorrect. It gives examples such as using reserved AS numbers or including only one AS in the set.

The resulting reduction in routing-table size was extremely small, according to the RFC, while the feature added complexity and impeded work on BGP security technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's analysis found little practical benefit from this kind of aggregation. It says the small table-size reduction did not justify the added complexity.

sections.title: Recommendation to Operators
sections.content:
The RFC RECOMMENDS that operators not create new announcements containing AS_SET or AS_CONFED_SET. If they have already announced such routes, they SHOULD withdraw them and announce the component prefixes without AS_SET or AS_CONFED_SET.

The recommendation is about sending routes. The RFC does not prescribe what an operator should do when receiving a route that contains these segments, and it notes that operators should understand the effects of a change.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should stop sending routes with these segments. For existing routes, the RFC recommends withdrawing them and announcing the component prefixes separately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says avoiding AS_SET can reduce rarely used BGP complexity and code, thereby reducing attack surface. It also says this can simplify the design and implementation of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure and systems that rely on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Removing rarely used path-segment handling can reduce implementation complexity. The RFC also connects the change to simpler RPKI design and implementation.
